cards.front: What is the fundamental principle that allows any linear transformation $T: V \to W$ to be represented by a matrix?
cards.back: A linear transformation $T$ is completely determined by its action on a basis of the domain space $V$. If we know $T(\mathbf{b}_1), T(\mathbf{b}_2), \dots, T(\mathbf{b}_n)$ for a basis $B = \{\mathbf{b}_1, \dots, \mathbf{b}_n\}$ of $V$, then $T(\mathbf{v})$ can be found for any $\mathbf{v} \in V$ by linearity.

cards.front: Given a linear transformation $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$, how do you construct its standard matrix $[T]$?
cards.back:
The columns of the standard matrix $[T]$ are the images of the standard basis vectors of $\mathbb{R}^n$ under $T$. Specifically, if $\mathbf{e}_j$ is the $j$-th standard basis vector of $\mathbb{R}^n$, then the $j$-th column of $[T]$ is $T(\mathbf{e}_j)$.
$$[T] = \begin{bmatrix} T(\mathbf{e}_1) & T(\mathbf{e}_2) & \dots & T(\mathbf{e}_n) \end{bmatrix}$$

cards.front: If $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is a linear transformation with standard matrix $A$, how do you compute $T(\mathbf{x})$ for any vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$?
cards.back: To compute $T(\mathbf{x})$, you simply multiply the standard matrix $A$ by the vector $\mathbf{x}$: $T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$. This is the core utility of the matrix representation.

cards.front: Find the standard matrix for the linear transformation $T: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ that rotates vectors counterclockwise by an angle $\theta$.
cards.back:
1. Find $T(\mathbf{e}_1)$: $T(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix}) = \begin{smallmatrix} \cos\theta \\ \sin\theta \end{smallmatrix}$.
2. Find $T(\mathbf{e}_2)$: $T(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix}) = \begin{smallmatrix} -\sin\theta \\ \cos\theta \end{smallmatrix}$.
3. The standard matrix is formed by these columns:
$$[T] = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$$

cards.front: Let $V$ and $W$ be finite-dimensional vector spaces with bases $B = \{\mathbf{b}_1, \dots, \mathbf{b}_n\}$ and $C = \{\mathbf{c}_1, \dots, \mathbf{c}_m\}$ respectively. How do you find the matrix $[T]_{C \leftarrow B}$ for $T: V \to W$?
cards.back:
The columns of the matrix $[T]_{C \leftarrow B}$ are the coordinate vectors of the images of the basis vectors of $V$ (under $T$) with respect to the basis $C$ of $W$. Specifically, the $j$-th column is $[T(\mathbf{b}_j)]_C$.
$$[T]_{C \leftarrow B} = \begin{bmatrix} [T(\mathbf{b}_1)]_C & [T(\mathbf{b}_2)]_C & \dots & [T(\mathbf{b}_n)]_C \end{bmatrix}$$
This matrix allows computing $[T(\mathbf{v})]_C = [T]_{C \leftarrow B} [\mathbf{v}]_B$.

cards.front: Is the matrix representation of a linear transformation unique? Explain.
cards.back: Yes, for a given choice of bases for the domain and codomain, the matrix representation of a linear transformation is unique. This is because a linear transformation is uniquely determined by its action on a basis, and the coordinate representation of each image vector with respect to the codomain basis is also unique.

cards.front: Let $T: V \to V$ be a linear operator. If $A = [T]_B$ is its matrix relative to basis $B$, and $P$ is the change-of-basis matrix from $C$ to $B$ (i.e., $P = [I]_{B \leftarrow C}$), how do you find $D = [T]_C$?
cards.back:
The matrix $D = [T]_C$ can be found using the similarity transformation:
$$D = P^{-1}AP$$
Here, $P^{-1}$ is the change-of-basis matrix from $B$ to $C$ (i.e., $P^{-1} = [I]_{C \leftarrow B}$). This formula connects the matrix representations of the same linear transformation under different bases.

cards.front: If $T_1: U \to V$ and $T_2: V \to W$ are linear transformations with matrices $[T_1]_{B_V \leftarrow B_U}$ and $[T_2]_{B_W \leftarrow B_V}$ respectively, what is the matrix representation for their composition $T_2 \circ T_1: U \to W$?
cards.back:
The matrix representation of the composite transformation $T_2 \circ T_1$ is the product of their individual matrices (in the correct order):
$$[T_2 \circ T_1]_{B_W \leftarrow B_U} = [T_2]_{B_W \leftarrow B_V} [T_1]_{B_V \leftarrow B_U}$$
This demonstrates that matrix multiplication corresponds to the composition of linear transformations.
